items.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We opened up in this little club called the Downbeat. J. J. [Johnson] on trombone.

ctx.x: You organized – sometimes for Miles you organized the bands for him? How did that work?

Yeah. I was working with him. Off and on different periods, Miles would call me, and I’d work with him through a particular period. At this time he was doing real bad. He was strung out real bad. He was pawning stuff. We opened up in this little club called the Downbeat. J. J. [Johnson] on trombone. I can’t remember the whole rhythm section. It might have been A. T. or somebody. But at any rate, somebody called his father. I don’t know if it was the club owner or whatever. One night we were playing. Miles was…

and got Miles’s coat. He was talking to the club owner for a minute, and they went out the door. So J. J. took over the band for the rest of the week, and Miles went home to his father. After he stayed down there and got his self together . . .

items.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: By the time of the Art Blakey ones, you were using Jackie McLean.

ctx.x: My question is this. You played with two of the major drummers. One was a carryover from your earlier experience, Kenny Clarke. The other was Art Blakey. By the time of the Art Blakey ones, you were using Jackie McLean. The question is this. I’m going to quote you [somebody's writing] from Down Beat magazine. I wonder what this person must think, looking back. It said, “J.J. Johnson’s group was on fire." I’m paraphrasing. It said, “And it was an all round great experience except the rude, unswinging drumming of…
